newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Islamic ministers meet to back Arafat on Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Islamic ministers meet to back Arafat on Jerusalem.

text.p: Islamic ministers on Thursday met in Rabat to support the Palestinians against Israel's settlement policy in Jerusalem, as U.S. envoy Dennis Ross flew to Israel to try to salvage the Middle East peace process.
Ross earlier on Thursday held what he called "very thorough" talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in Rabat and was to hold two meetings with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israel last week started building a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem and there have since been daily clashes in the West Bank between Palestinians and Israeli soldiers.
Late on Thursday ministers from the 16-member Al-Qods committee met in King Hassan's palace in the Moroccan capital.

The king, who had earlier met Arafat for private talks, and discussed developments in the Middle East with Ross, said the ministers were to examine a draft declaration issued by an Islamic summit in Islamabad earlier this month.

Arafat told ministers that Jerusalem faced "a dangerous operation of Judaisation". He accused Israel of trying to change the city's demography "in an attempt to change by force U.N. decisions and resolutions".
Azeddine Laraki, secretary-general of the 54-member Organisation of the Islamic Conference, said the draft referred to the "dangerous situation" facing Jerusalem from Israel's policy.
It was unclear whether the draft was to be the basis of a resolution from the Al-Qods meeting, chaired by King Hassan.

"The Israeli expansionist policy in Jerusalem and other Arab occupied territories...represents a dangerous threat to the peace process," Laraki quoted the draft as saying, adding it urgently called on Israel to stop its policy of settlements.
Laraki said the draft declared support for the Middle East peace process and previous agreements and commitments between Palestinians and Israel, based on the land-for-peace formula.

In a statement issued by the U.S. embassy, Ross said: "The purpose of my mission is to make an assessment of the situation in the Middle East for the President (Bill Clinton) and the secretary of state and to report back to them by this weekend."
Neither Ross nor Arafat made any comment to reporters after nearly two hours of talks, underlining the delicate task facing Clinton's envoy in salvaging the peace process.
Earlier Arafat and Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa made clear before Ross arrived at Arafat's villa that he would be left in no doubt over Arab anger with the policies of Netanyahu.
Moussa told reporters he had talked with the Saudi, Syrian, Gulf and North African foreign ministers -- in Rabat to attend the Al-Qods committee -- and had briefed Arafat on their views.

"Everybody, all of us, are really disturbed over what is going on in Jerusalem. This is the issue. This is the reason why all the repercussions which took place in the occupied territories and in the Middle East have occurred," he said.

Moussa emphasised the Arab view that Israeli policies were to blame for the crisis. "The problems lies, begins, stems from the policy of settlements in Jerusalem and in the occupied territories. We cannot accept a deviation from that point."
Israel sees Jerusalem as its eternal capital. The Palestinians say Arab East Jerusalem is the capital of their future state.

Members of the Al-Qods committee are Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Bangladesh, Guinea, Indonesia, Iran, Niger, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, Pakistan, Senegal, Iraq, Syria, Mauritania and the Palestinian Authority.
